newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French October jobless slips by 12,000.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French October jobless slips by 12,000.

text.p: French unemployment showed a surprise small drop in October, but the percentage out of work remained a record 12.6 percent, and economists predicted that the jobless total would stay high throughout 1997.
The number of unemployed fell in October by 12,000 or 0.4 percent from the previous month to 3,100,800, the Ministry of Labour reported on Monday. But the figure was up 5.3 percent year-on-year.
And the jobless rate according to International Labour Organisation criteria excluding those who did any work at all was unchanged at 12.6 percent.

The decline in the number of jobless gave some comfort to the conservative government, striving to cut unemployment in the face of weak growth at the same time as selling its austerity programme to allow France to qualify for European monetary union.
Prime Minister Alain Juppe, fighting growing unpopularity among voters, said the numbers were in the right direction but it was too early to draw conclusions from one month's data.
"It's encouraging but I will resist sounding triumphant," he told reporters on a visit to the northwestern city of Lille.
Private economists said at least two months of straight falls would be needed to suggest unemployment was on the wane.
"Despite the small fall in October, the underlying trend in unemployment appears steadily upwards," General Accident economist Andrew Milligan said.

The high unemployment was putting increasing pressure on the government to act, "hence the recent hints by some French officials for a weaker exchange rate against the dollar," said General Accident's Milligan.

Late last month, two Bank of France monetary policy council members and former president Valery Giscard d'Estaing called for a fall in the franc's exchange rate against the dollar, saying it would spur export industries and help create more jobs.
The calls reflected a general mood that Germany's attachment to a powerful currency was imposing too high a toll on European economies in the run-up to monetary union, economists said.

But economists said the debate over the franc's value ignored the core problem afflicting France's economy -- lack of flexibility in its job market reflected by high payroll charges and inability to hire and fire easily.
Economists said the drop was more likely a small correction after two months of big rises in unemployment.
"It's more month-to-month volatility. I really don't think it signals a change in the overall deterioration," said economist Sonja Gibbs of Nomura.

Economist David Naude of JP Morgan noted that unemployment had risen by nearly 70,000 over the previous two months "and here I think we're seeing the usual volatility, probably paybacks for the strong rises of the past months."

Unemployment has been languishing around 12.5 percent since the summer. While the government forecasts growth of 1.3 percent this year and 2.3 percent next year, economists said unemployment would still be around 12 percent throughout 1997.

"What's worrying is that the next couple of years are supposed to be recovery years for France, and if it stays around these levels, the next time there's a downturn, you'll end up at 13 percent or more," said one economist.
